The Roman Republic was born in 509 BCE from the ashes of the monarchy, a pivotal moment when the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled following the infamous rape of Lucretia by his son Sextus. This event catalyzed a profound political transformation, replacing the rule of a single monarch with a complex system of checks and balances designed to prevent tyranny. The new government was led by two consuls, elected annually by the citizens, who held supreme executive power but could veto each other, ensuring no single individual could dominate the state. Alongside the consuls stood the Senate, a body of former magistrates who advised on policy and controlled the treasury, and various popular assemblies that allowed citizens to vote on laws and elect officials. This foundational structure established the *res publica*—the "public affair"—as a collective endeavor, though in practice, political power remained heavily concentrated in the hands of the patrician aristocracy, setting the stage for centuries of internal social conflict.

CUDA graph replay accelerates execution primarily by eliminating the significant CPU-side overhead associated with launching kernels individually. In eager execution, every kernel launch requires the CPU to validate arguments, manage stream dependencies, and issue commands to the GPU driver, which can take several microseconds per launch. For workloads with many small kernels, this CPU latency often dominates the total execution time, leaving the GPU idle while waiting for instructions. CUDA graphs capture the entire sequence of operations—including kernel launches, memory copies, and synchronization points—into a static directed acyclic graph (DAG) beforehand. When replayed, the GPU executes this pre-compiled graph as a single atomic unit, drastically reducing the CPU-GPU synchronization overhead and allowing for tighter, more efficient scheduling of tasks on the device.

However, this performance gain comes with specific costs and constraints. The primary cost is the upfront overhead of capturing and instantiating the graph, which involves recording the execution sequence and optimizing it for the GPU. This makes CUDA graphs less suitable for dynamic workloads where the structure of the computation changes frequently or where kernels are launched only once. Additionally, graphs are generally static; while parameters can be updated, the topology of the graph (the number and order of nodes) cannot change without re-capturing. This rig
